claims.text: Local chemical disorder governs superconducting behavior in high-entropy superconducting alloys.
Lattice distortion governs superconducting behavior in high-entropy superconducting alloys.
Chemical disorder and lattice distortion control the effectiveness of electron–phonon coupling.
Electron–phonon coupling controls the formation and coherence of Cooper pairs in the proposed alloys.
Nb, Ta, and V are examples of superconducting constituent elements for the proposed high-entropy alloy.
A high-entropy alloy containing such elements can be synthesized as a disordered solid solution with significant lattice distortion.
Thermal or other processing can produce samples of nearly unchanged composition but different structural states.
Annealing will reduce local chemical disorder and lattice distortion in the proposed superconducting alloy.
Increased lattice distortion enhances electron scattering.
Enhanced electron scattering disrupts the electron–phonon interactions needed for Cooper-pair formation.
Reducing disorder promotes more effective electron–phonon coupling.
More effective electron–phonon coupling produces a higher superconducting transition temperature.
More effective electron–phonon coupling produces a larger superconducting gap.
Annealed, less-disordered samples will have higher Tc and a larger superconducting gap than as-synthesized, more-disordered samples.
The as-synthesized baseline will have lower Tc because disorder suppresses electron–phonon coupling.
The proposed relationship is expected to apply to superconducting-element high-entropy alloys that form disordered solid solutions.
The proposed relationship may not apply when pairing is nonconventional or dominated by magnetic interactions.
X-ray diffraction peak broadening and pair-distribution-function analysis can characterize the degree of lattice distortion.
Tunneling spectroscopy or ARPES can measure the superconducting gap in the comparison samples.
Failure of reduced-distortion samples to show a statistically significant enhancement in both Tc and superconducting gap is designated as falsifying the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The conditions state that experiments are performed below the expected transition temperature, whereas determining Tc by four-point resistivity normally requires a temperature sweep through the transition, including temperatures above it.
